about.title: About
about.description: A web application to analyze, safely edit, and move Terraform state across existing backends — with CI-driven drift detection and version testing.

landing.heroSubtitle: Track your Terraform estate across every backend — detect drift, validate version upgrades, schedule checks, and move state safely.
landing.step1DescAuth: You're signed in. Head to your dashboard for a cross-source overview of your estate.
landing.step1DescUnauth: Sign in with your organization's identity provider to access your Terraform estate.
landing.step2Desc: Add a state backend (S3, Azure, GCS, Terraform Cloud, and more) so the analyzer can index your state files.
landing.step3Desc: Run drift and version-lab checks, schedule recurring runs, generate reports, and transfer state between sources.

dashboard.title: Home
dashboard.body: A cross-source overview of your Terraform estate: total Resources Under Management (RUM), provider and resource-type breakdowns, and the Terraform version spread.

sections.p: RUM counts managed resource instances (count/for_each expansions included); data sources are tracked separately. Cards link to the pages where you can act.

Aggregation runs under a time budget with bounded concurrency. If a source is slow or unreachable (large HCP orgs, rate limits), the page renders what completed and the banner reports how many sources were skipped.

sources.title: Sources
sources.body: Connect existing state backends and work with their state files — nothing is migrated to use TSM; it reads the backends you already have.

sections.p: Local directories, HCP Terraform / Terraform Enterprise, S3, Azure Blob, GCS, Git, Consul, PostgreSQL, Kubernetes secrets, and the generic http backend. Credentials are encrypted at rest and never returned by the API.
Pick a source to list its states (type to filter long lists — HCP workspaces show their names). Tabs show analysis, per-resource inventory, raw JSON, and backups.
Raw edits and state operations (rm / mv) follow lock → backup → write → audit. Every write captures a restorable backup first, and the Backups tab can revert.
Analyze an uploaded .tfstate ad hoc without connecting a source — nothing is stored.

drift.title: Drift
drift.body: Dispatch a terraform plan through your CI to compare state against code and live infrastructure. Results return via a signed one-shot callback and render as a per-resource diff.

sections.p: Store an org-level credential once (ADO org/project or GitHub owner). Pipeline connections built from a source pick from its real pipelines/repos/workflows and share its token — rotate the PAT in one place.

The wizard takes a repo from zero to drift-enabled: pick source + repo, customize the workflow template, commit it manually or via an automated branch + PR (write-scoped PAT), then create the pipeline definition and connection in one step.

Dispatch targets must be created from the TSM workflow template — it declares the parameters TSM sends and posts results back. Regular CI pipelines reject the dispatch with an 'unexpected parameter' error.

Leave the ref empty to run from the pipeline's default branch. The CI job must be able to reach the TSM callback URL — hosted agents cannot reach a localhost deployment; use a tunnel (TSM_SERVER_CALLBACK_URL) or a self-hosted agent.

versionLab.title: Version Lab
versionLab.body: Test whether your Terraform code plans cleanly against a pinned Terraform version — and optionally pinned provider/module versions or a registry mirror — by dispatching init/plan to CI.

sections.p: Runs dispatch through the same pipeline connections and must target a pipeline created from the version-health workflow template (Workflow template button).
init ✓/✗ and plan ✓/✗ show which phase failed; healthy means both passed with the pinned versions. Use this before upgrading Terraform or providers across your estate.

reports.title: Reports
reports.body: Filter analyzed state files across every source — by Terraform version, provider, resource type, size, and resource counts — then export the matches as Markdown, JSON, or CSV.

sections.p: Exports are audited. To report on a single state file in depth, open its detail view on the Sources page (MD/JSON/CSV buttons).

transfer.title: Transfer
transfer.body: Copy (backup) or move (migrate) a state file between sources — e.g. local to S3, or HCP to a new backend.

sections.p: Migrate verifies serial, lineage, and resource-count parity on the target after the copy. A failed verification leaves the source untouched and is flagged.
Optionally empty the original after a verified migrate. It requires type-to-confirm, and a backup of the source is captured first so the operation is recoverable.
Destinations default to the state's friendly name with .tfstate appended — file-based targets only list *.tfstate files.

apiDocs.title: API Docs
apiDocs.body: Interactive OpenAPI documentation generated from the backend's handler annotations. Raw spec:

sections.p: Requests run with your session cookie; mutations carry the CSRF token automatically. The Sections rail tracks scrolling and jumps between tag groups.

schedules.title: Schedules
schedules.body: Cron-driven recurring drift runs. Each schedule dispatches its configured drift target on a cadence and records the last outcome.

sections.p: Standard 5-field cron expressions, or the shorthands daily, weekly, and every <duration> (minimum 1 minute). Next-run is computed server-side.
A schedule points at a pipeline connection plus optional source/state/ref/working-dir — the same inputs as a manual drift run. Run now triggers it immediately without disturbing the cadence.
Pair schedules with notification channels (Administration → Notifications) to get webhook/Slack alerts on drift or failures.

admin.title: Admin
admin.body: Identity management overview — user, organization, and role counts from the shared identity service. Cards link to the management pages.

adminUsers.title: Users
adminUsers.body: Manage user accounts: search, create, rename, delete, and manage per-organization role memberships from the edit dialog.

sections.p: Each chip is an organization membership colored by role template. Tooltips show the full org/role.

Export downloads everything attributed to a user (profile, memberships, audit entries). Erase anonymizes PII, clears the IdP subject so re-login cannot resurrect the account, and revokes memberships — audit history stays, attributed to an anonymized id. Erase requires typing the user's email.
Memberships granted via group mappings are reconciled at each login — manual changes to those organizations will be overwritten or revoked to match the IdP.

adminOrganizations.title: Organizations
adminOrganizations.body: Create and manage organizations, their IdP bindings, and their members.

sections.p: Binding an organization to oidc/saml/ldap (optionally a named IdP) restricts which provider's logins may map into it.
View members opens the roster: add users (with an optional role template), change roles inline, or remove members.

adminRoles.title: Roles
adminRoles.body: The role templates and the permission scopes they grant. System roles (viewer, analyst, operator, editor, admin) are predefined.

sections.p: The reference table explains every scope. Expand a role to see its scopes and a category-by-category breakdown — admin grants everything.

adminOidc.title: OIDC Groups
adminOidc.body: Map IdP groups to organization roles. These mappings are runtime-editable and take effect on the next login.

sections.p: Saved settings here override the file configuration entirely (including an empty mapping list). The group claim name falls back to the file config, then 'groups'.

Organizations referenced by any mapping are IdP-authoritative: losing the group revokes the membership at next login. Unmapped organizations are never touched, and the default role applies only on first login.
Their mappings are shown read-only — they are configured in the server config file but reconcile with the same deprovisioning semantics.

adminMtls.title: mTLS Certificates
adminMtls.body: Read-only view of mutual-TLS client-certificate authentication: whether it is enabled, the client CA, and certificate-subject → scope mappings (configured in the server config file).

adminSso.title: SSO
adminSso.body: Read-only aggregate of every identity provider: OIDC, SAML (per-IdP), LDAP, mTLS, and the SCIM provisioning toggle — enabled state, key configuration, and group mappings. Secrets are never shown.

adminNotifications.title: Notifications
adminNotifications.body: Webhook and Slack channels fired on drift-detected and run-failed events.

sections.p: Destination URLs are stored encrypted and never returned — the form shows only whether a destination exists; leaving it blank on edit keeps the current one. Use Test to send a sample message.

adminAudit.title: Audit Log
adminAudit.body: Every mutation across the app lands here with actor and IP attribution: identity changes, source/state/backup/transfer operations, report generation, run dispatches, schedules, notification channels, and CI integrations.

sections.p: Only successful actions are recorded; failed attempts return errors but do not log. GDPR-erased users keep their history under an anonymized identifier.
Filter by date range, resource type, action (partial match), or user email. Export downloads the filtered set as CSV or JSON (capped at 1000 rows). Click a row for full detail including metadata.

adminApiKeys.title: API Keys
adminApiKeys.body: Self-service Bearer credentials (tsm_…) for CI pipelines and scripts — drift ingest, state reads, anything the API offers. Everyone manages their own keys; admins see all keys. A key may only carry scopes its creator holds. The secret is shown exactly once at creation; rotation can keep the old key valid for up to 72 hours while consumers switch over.
